The manipulation of time in this excerpt—the famous opening of Franz Kafka's *The Metamorphosis*—is masterfully balanced to serve the story's tone and themes. 

Initially, the narrative **stretches time**. In the real world, waking up and glancing around one's bedroom takes only a few seconds. However, the author draws out this brief moment over two full paragraphs, delving into minute details about Gregor's transformed body, the fabric samples on his desk, and the framed magazine picture on his wall. This stretching of time creates a surreal, dreamlike pacing that contrasts the horrifying absurdity of his transformation with the mundane, everyday details of his life, effectively grounding the reader in Gregor's disoriented mindset.

In the final paragraph, the narrative shifts to **compression of time**. Gregor attempts to roll onto his right side "wohl hundertmal" (probably a hundred times) until he begins to feel a dull pain. Instead of describing each attempt in real-time, the author condenses this prolonged, repetitive struggle into a single sentence. This compression effectively conveys the futility and exhaustion of his efforts without bogging down the narrative pace. 

Together, the stretching of his initial realization and the compression of his physical struggle create an appropriate, engaging rhythm that highlights both his psychological shock and his physical helplessness.
